analysis.one_liner: Restores federal Clean Water Act protection to all US waters, including wetlands and small streams.
analysis.headline: The Clean Water Authority Restoration Act never got a committee vote in the Senate before Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: After two Supreme Court rulings narrowed which waters the Clean Water Act covers, this bill would replace the term 'navigable waters' with 'waters of the United States' throughout the law, clearly extending federal pollution protection to wetlands, ponds, and small streams — including ones that never cross state lines. The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink water drawn from lakes, streams, and groundwater; communities that count on wetlands to absorb floods; and the fishing and outdoor recreation economies that depend on clean water. Developers and polluting industries currently discharge into small streams and wetlands with less federal oversight; this bill would subject those discharges to permits again.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'waters of the United States' to cover all interstate and intrastate waters, their tributaries, wetlands, and intermittent streams, restoring pollution controls across them [S2] [S3].
States the purpose as protecting waters 'to the fullest extent of the legislative authority of Congress under the Constitution,' reversing narrowed jurisdiction from court decisions [S2] [S3].
Notes that millions rely on these waters to filter drinking water supplies, protect health, and create economic opportunity [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Developers, farming operations, and industrial polluters who would once again need federal permits to fill or discharge into wetlands, small streams, ponds, and other formerly protected waters. The bill preserves states' rights to run their own permitting programs [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches 'to the fullest extent' of Congress's power, covering even waters that never leave one state; critics argue this raises federal permitting costs for farms, builders, and small landowners and was an expansive reading of constitutional authority [S3].
A broader jurisdictional scope could mean more federal permits and compliance costs for anyone discharging into or filling protected waters [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and flood-protection benefits of restoring clean water protection are large and widely shared, while the costs fall on parties discharging into formerly protected waters. But the bill as written is a maximalist reading of federal power that invites legal and political resistance; narrower or phased approaches could achieve much of the same protection with less friction. [S3]

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it died at the end of the 109th Congress in January 2007.

narrative.text: Introduced April 27, 2005 by Sen. Feingold with nine original cosponsors, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee [S1] [S3] [S5].
The committee never held a hearing or markup, and no vote was ever taken in either chamber before Congress ended January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Developers, industrial polluters, and agricultural operations avoided renewed federal permitting requirements over wetlands, ponds, and small streams. Communities relying on those waters for drinking supplies, flood control, and recreation saw no change. [S3]

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled Senate committee took no action.

industries.note: Would face federal Clean Water Act permitting requirements again for filling or building on wetlands, ponds, and small streams that had fallen outside federal jurisdiction.
Discharges into formerly protected waters would again require federal permits and compliance with pollution limits.
Farm operations near wetlands, potholes, and intermittent streams could face additional federal oversight, though the bill leaves existing state permitting programs in place.
